summary: The alleged form of theft matters. Larceny involves taking another person's property without consent, intending at the time to deprive the owner permanently or for long enough to lose a major part of its value or enjoyment, and moving and keeping it even briefly. Theft by trick involves knowing the property belongs to someone else, obtaining possession through fraud or deceit with that deprivation intent, and keeping it for some time; the owner did not intend to transfer ownership. Theft by false pretense instead involves knowing and intentional deception to induce transfer of both possession and ownership, with the owner's actual reliance on the deception. False pretense also has special proof requirements: a false writing or token, a signed or handwritten memorandum, or two witnesses or one witness with corroborating evidence, as specified in section 532(b). A broken promise alone does not prove an original intent to deceive. These are alternative theories, not a combined checklist that must all be proved; the charging papers and facts determine which theory is alleged. Other theft theories, defenses and special proof rules may require separate review.
elements: The prosecution must establish the applicable theft theory, not merely that property is worth $950 or less.
Larceny: nonconsensual taking with the required intent to deprive, movement and possession even briefly.

Trick: knowing another owns the property, fraud-induced possession without transfer of ownership, intent to deprive permanently or of a major portion of value or enjoyment, and keeping it for some time.
False pretense: intentional deception inducing possession and ownership through reliance, with the applicable section 532(b) proof requirements.
The value, type of property and prior-conviction allegations must also fit the applicable petty-theft grading rules.
mentalState: Theory-specific: the required intent to deprive for larceny or trick; knowing, intentional deception to induce transfer of possession and ownership for false pretense. Mere nonperformance is not enough.

searchAliases: Soliciting or Agreeing to Engage in Prostitution
summary: The alleged conduct matters: engaging in an act, soliciting, and agreeing are alternative theories, not one combined checklist. For the engaging theory, CALCRIM 1153 describes willingly engaging in sexual intercourse or a lewd act with another person in exchange for money or other compensation. A lewd act for this purpose involves touching the genitals, buttocks, or female breast of either participant with part of the other participant's body for sexual arousal or gratification of either person. These engaging-act requirements should not be treated as a requirement that the sexual act was completed in a solicitation or agreement case. An agreement requires specific intent, acceptance of an offer or solicitation, and an additional act in California in furtherance by the person accepting. The receiving-compensation, paying-an-adult, and paying-a-minor branches must be distinguished. Section 647(b) does not apply to a child under 18 alleged to have engaged in conduct to receive money or other consideration. The exact subdivision and the separate age, knowledge, payment, and prior-conviction conditions still control the applicable punishment.
elements: Identify whether the allegation is solicitation, agreement, or engaging in an act, and whether it concerns receiving compensation, paying an adult, or paying a minor.
Engaging theory: willingly engaging in sexual intercourse or a lewd act with another person in exchange for money or other compensation; lewd touching requires the specified sexual purpose.
Agreement theory: acceptance with specific intent to engage, plus an additional act in California in furtherance by the person accepting; acceptance alone is insufficient.
Section 647(b)(5) excludes children under 18 alleged to have engaged in conduct to receive money or other consideration.
The engaging-act explanation does not supply an exhaustive elements checklist for solicitation or the separate sentencing branches.
mentalState: Theory-specific: willingly or on purpose for engaging, with sexual arousal or gratification as the purpose of lewd touching; specific intent to engage for agreement. Receiving compensation requires the intent specified in section 647(b)(1). Do not substitute this bounded explanation for the elements of the exact charged subdivision.
